name: Lenomorelin (Ghrelin)

lead: Ghrelin (INN lenomorelin) is the stomach hormone that signals hunger and prompts growth hormone release. Fat-loss and muscle communities discuss it because appetite and GH both shape body fat and muscle.

Once an octanoyl group is attached by the enzyme GOAT, ghrelin activates the GHS-R1a receptor in the brain, pituitary and gut, driving hunger and GH release. Administered ghrelin has been studied clinically in settings such as cancer cachexia and frailty. No study has tested it for appearance goals.

paras: Outside clinical research it appears mainly in discussions of appetite and GH rather than as a routine anyone follows. Its main clinical use has been to stimulate appetite and weight in wasting conditions.

Clinical use has been investigational. The sources reviewed give no safety summary, and it is not an approved appearance treatment. Because it raises hunger, effects on appetite run opposite to fat-loss goals.

angle.text: Ghrelin is the stomach hormone that raises hunger and stimulates growth hormone, so fat-loss and muscle communities discuss it as a lever on appetite and body composition. It has been studied in cachexia and frailty, not for cosmetic use.

lead: Ghrelin, whose international nonproprietary name is lenomorelin, is a peptide hormone made mainly by enteroendocrine cells of the stomach. It is widely called the "hunger hormone" because it raises the drive to eat, and it also stimulates growth hormone release from the pituitary, which gave it its name.[1]

It is identified in 1999 as the ligand of the growth hormone secretagogue receptor.[1][2] Its relevance to looksmaxxing lies in body composition: appetite, fat mass and growth hormone. Administered ghrelin has been studied in clinical settings such as cancer cachexia and frailty, not as a cosmetic agent.[3][4][5]

paras: Ghrelin acts on GHS-R1a, found in the hypothalamus, pituitary, vagus nerve and gastrointestinal tract, mediating growth hormone release, hunger, glucose and lipid metabolism and gut motility. It activates neuropeptide Y and AgRP neurons that drive appetite.[1] In animal studies it raises food intake mainly by increasing meal frequency.[1]

Ghrelin becomes active when an octanoyl group is attached to its third serine residue by the enzyme ghrelin O-acyltransferase (GOAT).[1][6] The desacyl form does not activate GHS-R1a but has other effects, and both forms occur in stomach tissue.[1][7]

Blood levels peak before meals and fall after eating, and stomach expression rises with fasting.[1][8] Levels are lower in obesity and after gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy, and higher in anorexia nervosa, Prader-Willi syndrome and cancer cachexia.[1][9] A New England Journal of Medicine study of 50 overweight or obese patients reported that hormonal adaptations to diet-induced weight loss, including changes in appetite-related hormones, persisted for a year.[10]

Registered studies have examined ghrelin administration in cancer-related appetite loss (a phase 3 study of 30 patients and a phase 1/2 cachexia study of 21), frailty in ageing, cystic fibrosis, stroke, peripheral artery disease (unacylated form), alcohol craving, sleep and sympathetic nervous system effects in healthy volunteers and people with obesity.[3][4][5][11][12] Wikipedia states that evidence is insufficient to say whether ghrelin helps manage cachexia.[1] No studies found of ghrelin for cosmetic or appearance goals.
Related work includes the unacylated-ghrelin analogue livoletide, studied for hyperphagia in Prader-Willi syndrome.[1] Animal studies suggest possible cardioprotective effects.[1]

timeline.event: Ghrelin identified as the endogenous ligand of the GH secretagogue receptor.[1]
Acylated and des-acyl forms characterised in gastrointestinal tissue.[7]
The enzyme GOAT, which octanoylates ghrelin, identified.[6]
